title: Cornish Saffron Buns
subtitle: enriched yeasted buns coloured with saffron
excerpt: Cornish saffron buns are yeasted enriched buns made yellow with steeped saffron, dotted with currants and mixed peel. They are softer and slightly sweeter than regular bread rolls, with a fragrant, slightly floral flavour from the saffron. Makes 12.
sourceNotes: Saffron was imported into Cornwall through the tin trade with the Mediterranean from at least the 16th century, and saffron buns and saffron cake have been Cornish specialities ever since. Mrs Beeton (1861, Project Gutenberg #10136) gives a saffron cake recipe. Edith Martin, Cornish Recipes Ancient and Modern (1929, reprinted by the Cornwall Federation of Women's Institutes), gives both a saffron cake (loaf format) and saffron buns (individual rolls), both using yeast-leavened enriched dough. The saffron is steeped in hot water or milk before being added to the dough to distribute its colour evenly.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked buns, wrapped. Warm in a low oven for 10 minutes from frozen.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The saffron should be steeped in the milk at least 30 minutes before starting, or overnight in the fridge for a deeper colour.

glossaryTerms.definition: The dried stigmas of the Crocus sativus flower, used to colour and flavour food. A small pinch steeped in warm liquid turns the liquid a vivid yellow-orange. Saffron is expensive; the colour and flavour are genuine and cannot be replicated with turmeric, which gives only colour.

content.text: buns have a bright yellow crumb from saffron steeped in warm milk. The flavour is subtle: slightly floral and honeyed, different enough from a plain currant bun to be distinctive without being overwhelmed. The dough is enriched with butter and egg, which gives the buns a soft, slightly brioche-like texture.

The saffron should be steeped for at least 30 minutes. The longer it steeps, the deeper the colour. After that the process is standard enriched dough: knead, first rise, shape, second rise, bake. The buns glaze well with a sugar and water syrup brushed on as they come out of the oven.

Add {{saffron}} of saffron threads to {{whole-milk}} of warm milk. Stir and leave for at least 30 minutes. The milk will turn a deep yellow-orange. Strain out the threads if preferred, or leave them in.

Combine {{strong-bread-flour}} of strong bread flour, {{fast-action-yeast}} of fast-action yeast, {{caster-sugar}} of caster sugar, and {{salt-table}} of salt in a large bowl or stand mixer. Add the saffron milk and the egg. Mix to a rough dough, then add {{unsalted-butter}} of softened butter a piece at a time and knead for 8 to 10 minutes until smooth and elastic.
Add {{currants}} of currants and {{mixed-peel}} of mixed peel and knead briefly to incorporate. Cover and leave to rise for 1 to 1.5 hours until doubled.
Divide the dough into 12 equal pieces. Shape each into a smooth round ball. Place on lined baking trays, spaced 4 cm apart. Cover loosely and prove for 30 to 45 minutes until puffed.

Heat the oven to 190°C fan (210°C conventional). Bake the buns for 15 to 18 minutes until golden. Mix the sugar with boiling water to make a glaze. Brush over the buns immediately as they come out of the oven. Cool on a wire rack.

items.symptom: Buns are pale yellow rather than bright golden
items.cause: Saffron steeped for too short a time, or too little saffron
items.fix: Steep for at least 30 minutes. More saffron and longer steeping give a deeper colour. Do not substitute turmeric; the flavour will be wrong.

items.symptom: Dough is sticky and hard to work
items.cause: Too much milk or butter not fully incorporated
items.fix: Add butter gradually. Enriched doughs are naturally softer than bread dough. Knead until smooth; a scraper helps with sticky dough.

items.symptom: Buns do not rise during proving
items.cause: Yeast killed by milk that was too hot
items.fix: The milk should be warm, not hot: about 37°C. Too hot kills the yeast; the dough will not rise at all.

content.text: Saffron baking in Cornwall predates most other British baked goods by several centuries. The saffron came via Cornish ports trading tin and copper for Mediterranean goods, including spices. Saffron cake and saffron buns are still baked and sold in Cornish bakeries today, where they are a point of local pride. The buns are slightly sticky from the glaze, soft inside, and have a flavour that is unlike any other British bun. They are best eaten fresh and warm, split and buttered.
